addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah

Entries are in **strict priority rank**, #1 highest, descending. Reprioritize by moving an
entry, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber. The numbers are positional rank,
not stable IDs. To refer to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention; a numbered
list item has no anchor to link to), not its number. Long-tail entries live in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper detail goes in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

     - the grade block: env warmup/bench vs run rows, per-signal letters, the settle cell
     - the -v warmup table and its exit/window/clock summary line

     - grade A certifies internal consistency of the state the run held, not a canonical number

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)
before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Close the records, so the later steps find them done:
   - backfill the chores/ladder refs of the commits the previous push made permanent
   - append this commit's chores rung + narrative (or its `TODO.md` block, under a one-home
     override)
   - bump the version-of-record
5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
6. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
7. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`), per the protocol's
[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a one-line `## Done` entry with its chores
   `[N]` ref.
2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
3. Full validation, mandatory.
4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
6. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for
   the commits the previous push made permanent; never record a SHA that is not on a permanent
   branch.

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

> - `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
>   is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
>   first parent.
> - `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
>   second parent.
> - `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
> 
> The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
> because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
> remains is reshaping and publishing them:
> 
> 1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
>    - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
>    `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
> 2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
>    - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
>    argument order.
> 3. `jj new <closeout>`
>    -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
> 4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
>    - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
>    it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
>    repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
>    separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
> 
> **Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
> close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
> none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
> time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
> from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
> stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
> requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
> but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
> different operation from committing and publishing, and only
> the latter is push's job.
> 
> #### Details
> 
> - **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
>   -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
>   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
>   is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
>   `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
>   a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
>   once published.
> - **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
>   or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
>   and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
>   rung, not the last close-out.
> - **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
>   follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
>   leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
>   re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
>   parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
>   on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
>   content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
>   back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
>   commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
>   publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
> - **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
>   SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
>   in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
>   reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
> - **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
>   becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
>   pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
>   [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
>   SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
> - **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
>   bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
>   does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
>   push force-updates the target.
> - **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
>   the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
>   from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
>   tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
>   squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
> 
> #### Recovery
> 
> - **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
>   reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
> - **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
>   fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
>   Do not push a shape you did not intend; after step 4 the
>   remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
> - **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
>   `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
>   affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
>   made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
>   rebase onto the merge.
> - **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
>   `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
>   If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
>   sideways move, not a rewrite.

> ## Grammar and storage
> 
> One prose spelling everywhere (ladders, chores, commit
> bullets, conversation):
> 
> ```
> <public>[-<suffix>]
> ```
> 
> - `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
> - `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters
>   or digits; usually integers (`3`, `3.1`, `3.1.0`), an
>   alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed, sparingly.
> - **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that
>   opens the suffix: never a dash inside the suffix, never a
>   `+` in the prose form. This is the portability invariant
>   that makes the version storable in every medium below.
> - **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**:
>   commit bullets and prose may write `v0.78.0-3.1` for
>   scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440
>   ignores a leading `v`; Cargo rejects one.)
> 
> Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
> 
> - **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim; the
>   suffix rides in the prerelease slot, valid at any dot
>   depth.
> - **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`:
>   `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`. Mechanical and bijective
>   because there is exactly one dash to find.
> - **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one
>   `-`; else the `+` remap; a new medium adds its case to
>   [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
> 
> Two reservations keep the remap sound:
> 
> - **The stored version identifies; it does not order.**
>   SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before* its bare release
>   (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out);
>   PEP 440 sorts the remapped form *after* it, and
>   reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite
>   directions, so no cross-medium logic may compare stored
>   versions; ordering truth lives in the ladder and git
>   history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a
>   version gate) is unaffected.
> - **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer
>   build-metadata use in Rust repos even though Cargo allows
>   it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with
>   the Python spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares
>   the deviation in its `custom.md`.
> 
> **Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a
> sibling repo rejected every multi-dash version outright, and
> the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
> 2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`,
> `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second `+` are all
> invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any
> depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but silently becomes the
> post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is
> the largest form every medium accepts.
>

> 
> ## Dev artifact name
> 
> When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the
> installed CLI) while this repo is under active development,
> the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle
> install never clobbers the binary consumers are running:
> 
> - **Name** — the manifest's package name carries a `-dev`
>   suffix (`vc-x1` → `vc-x1-dev`); if Rust, `[package].name`,
>   so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces
>   `<name>-dev` and leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
> - **Constant, not per-step** — the step already lives in the
>   version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V` reports the exact rung);
>   a per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and
>   litter the install dir with stale binaries.
> - **Promotion** — plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit
>   act: a separate clone built at the chosen commit with the
>   plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the
>   per-commit flow's install.
> 
> This project adopted the convention 2026-07-23 (during
> 0.75.0); projects without external consumers can skip it.

# AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260803-notes.md - provenance for the 20260803 baseline

What the 20260803 snapshot changes relative to 20260802, and why. Authored 2026-08-03 by
vc-x1's agent at wink's direction as a **baseline from vc-x1's perspective**: iiac-perf
reviews and refines, and the amended directory becomes the adoption base at convergence
(the 0730 proposal-review-adopt pattern). The three-repo evidence is
[pin-set-dedup-review-20260803.md](pin-set-dedup-review-20260803.md).

## Changes vs 20260802

- **Pin set grows by two files**: `notes/cycle-protocol.md` and `notes/versioning.md` move
  into `agent-data/`, so the pin-set boundary is the directory boundary and
  `diff -r agent-data/` catches all protocol drift. The `notes/` directory becomes records
  only.
  - cycle-protocol.md: vc-x1's copy is the base (trapezoid recipe, ladder-form chores, the
    0802 amendments), plus the changes below
  - versioning.md: vc-x1's copy, the only one carrying the 2026-07-30 "Grammar and storage"
    protocol (iiac-perf's and the payload's forked silently without it)
  - both gain the standard "Universal file, pinned..." header line
- **AGENTS.md file map**: the two files join the agent-data list; the records section is
  reworded to "records only, never universal rules".
- **cycle.md renamed cycle-checklists.md** (wink, at the 2026-08-03 adoption review): beside
  the newly pinned cycle-protocol.md the old name read as a scope collision; the new pair
  states the roles (act-time checklists vs full protocol with rationale and recovery). The
  files stay separate: hard rule 7's re-read-before-acting needs a file that is small and
  complete, and the protocol's recovery/rationale is exactly what act-time reads should skip.
  Only AGENTS.md linked the old name (five links, re-pointed).
- **jj.md gains two sections**:
  - "Revsets": the addressing primer condensed from jj-tips.md, so pinned files never link
    outside the pin set (cycle-protocol.md's `#revsets` links now target it)
  - "Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged": the 2026-08-03
    refinement of "treated as permanent, never rebased"; evidence in vc-x1's custom.md
    dogfood log
- **cycle-protocol.md, beyond the move**:
  - "Reviewing changes" gains the no-preflight-while-a-review-iterates rule, salvaged from
    vc-x1's `notes/draft-reviews.md` (2026-04-28), which then deletes
  - links re-pointed: agent-data siblings flatten, `jj-tips.md#revsets` becomes
    `jj.md#revsets`
- **jj-tips.md leaves the per-repo payload**: one copy now lives at the template root
  (reference material, not protocol; its three per-repo copies had drifted).
- **The dogfood log moves out of custom.md into `notes/dogfood.md`** (wink, 2026-08-03): the
  log is a record (dated evidence, append-only), so under records-only it belongs in notes/,
  and custom.md loses its one section that could never converge. With the log out, matching
  the template's custom.md skeleton becomes custom.md's healthy steady state, and drift from
  the skeleton is a visible signal of project content accumulating. AGENTS.md's custom.md
  section and records list amended; the payload seeds `work/notes/dogfood.md` with the birth
  entry.

## What this baseline drops from iiac-perf's copy, deliberately

The baseline takes vc-x1's cycle-protocol.md, which describes the current (0.78.0, in-process
jj-lib) binary. iiac-perf's copy carries material tied to the older spawn-based binary it
still runs; the baseline drops it from the *pinned* file, not from existence:

- the "Merge non-ff recipe" (merge set up before the push): superseded by the trapezoid
  recipe, which reshapes between two pushes
- "Clear push's saved state" recovery (`.vc-x1/push-state.toml`, `--restart`): the in-process
  push keeps no saved state
- the 0.22.0 empty-commit post-mortem (vc-x1 push after a manual merge setup): tied to the
  old recipe; valuable history that belongs in iiac-perf's own notes/ as a project record if
  it wants to keep it visible

Adoption for iiac-perf is therefore coupled to the family binary upgrade already on the
tier-2 agenda; until it upgrades, its old-binary operational notes live in its custom.md or
notes/, not in the pinned set.

## Review asks for iiac-perf

- the two jj.md additions (revset primer wording, bookmark discipline)
- the drop-list above: anything the old-binary material covers that the baseline loses and
  should not
- the tier-2 items still open on your agenda (one-home, every-commit-belongs-to-a-cycle,
  scope-based version advancement): decide whether any land in this same snapshot before
  adoption

content.content:
If hidden commits are specified, their ancestors also become available to the
search space. They are included in `all()`, `x..`, `~x`, etc., but not in
`..visible_heads()`, etc. For example, `hidden_id | all()` is equivalent to
`hidden_id | ::(hidden_id | visible_heads())`.
--
     `x::visible_heads()` if no hidden revisions are mentioned.
   * `x..`: Revisions that are not ancestors of `x`. Equivalent to `~::x`, and
     `x..visible_heads()` if no hidden revisions are mentioned.
   * `::x`: Ancestors of `x`, including the commits in `x` itself. Shorthand for
     `root()::x`.
--
   * `x::y`: Descendants of `x` that are also ancestors of `y`. Equivalent
      to `x:: & ::y`. This is what `git log` calls `--ancestry-path x..y`.
   * `x..y`: Ancestors of `y` that are not also ancestors of `x`. Equivalent to
     `::y ~ ::x`. This is what `git log` calls `x..y` (i.e. the same as we call it).
     Note that this is *not* a "path" between `x` and `y` in the commit graph -- `x`
     and `y` do not need to be related by ancestry.
--

    **Operator** `x..`

    * `D..` ⇒ `{}` (empty set)
--

    **Operator** `x..y`

    * `D..D` ⇒ `{}` (empty set)

The pinned set in `work/` is byte-identical to the 20260803 snapshot (work/ just adds the rest of the init payload), so this review covers both. Here it is, from iiac-perf's perspective.

## Review: the 20260803 baseline (template `work/` payload)

**Overall: sound, and I'd adopt it — the structure changes are things our own dogfood log asked for. Four concrete defects to fix before it becomes the adoption base, and one real sequencing decision (the binary coupling).**

### Endorsed without reservation

- **Pin set = directory boundary.** `cycle-protocol.md` and `versioning.md` moving into `agent-data/` means one `diff -r agent-data/` catches all protocol drift — exactly the "drift is a diff, not a mystery" promise, which the silent versioning.md fork proved `notes/` couldn't keep.
- **`cycle.md` -> `cycle-checklists.md` rename.** The pair now names its roles; hard rule 7's act-time re-read wants the small file, and the split preserves that.
- **Dogfood log -> `notes/dogfood.md`.** Right call. Our custom.md is currently ~60% dogfood log; with it out, "matching the skeleton is the healthy steady state" becomes genuinely checkable here.
- **The trapezoid recipe as written.** Push-linearly-then-reshape is exactly what our 0.23.0 post-facto experiment validated (chids and ochids survived, bookmark followed the rewrite), so the recipes' old disagreement resolves in favor of the mechanics we already tested. The Details/Recovery subsections (verify two parents, `<base>` is not always the previous close-out, step 4 moves the bookmark sideways so backfill must wait) encode real failure modes.
- **Bookmark discipline** (merge-only default, coordinated rewrites as escape hatch, deletable once merged). Consistent with our 2026-08-01 renumber — that was a coordinated rewrite, allowed under this wording — and it licenses cleaning up our merged bookmarks.
- **versioning.md "Grammar and storage".** No conflict with our usage (single dash, integer suffixes, no `+`); we get the protocol we silently lacked. The "Dev artifact name" section's skip clause applies to us — no external consumers of the iiac-perf binary.

### Defects found (fix in the snapshot before adoption)

1. **Stale step number in the custom.md skeleton.** `work/custom.md` says Full validation runs at "per-commit checklist step 4", but the renumbered checklist puts "Close the records" at 4 and validation at **5**. Our own custom.md carries the same stale number and needs the same fix at sync.
2. **Revset primer: the `X..` gloss is wrong.** jj.md says "`X..` descendants excluding X", but per `jj help -k revsets`, `x..` is "revisions that are **not ancestors** of x" (`~::x`) — in a repo with side branches (like ours) it includes commits that are not descendants of X at all. Descendants-excluding-X is `X:: ~ X`. The `X::`, `::X`, `..X` glosses are correct.
3. **prose.md violates its own width rule.** Two lines exceed 100 columns, both introduced by the recent amendments: line 19 (106 chars, the full-width application splice) and line 71 (134 chars, the "prohibition is on authoring" rewording). A rewrap fixes both.

content.text:
Found the root: the template-root `jj-tips.md` teaches the same thing — line 283 "`@..` is the *open* form: descendants of @, **excluding** @" and line 334 "`w..` descendants of w, excluding w" — so the pinned primer faithfully condensed a tutorial that already carried the house interpretation. This isn't a one-line typo in jj.md; it's the family's documented mental model of `..`, and it disagrees with the tool.

My opinion: you're right, and ASAP is the correct urgency. Three reasons, one reframe, and a scope note.

**Reason 1: there's no real choice to make.** jj implements `x..` as `~::x` regardless of what our docs say. A "house semantics" can only ever exist in prose, so keeping it doesn't give you the semantics you preferred — it gives you docs that are wrong about the tool you're driving. The only question was ever *when* the divergence bites, not whether.

**Reason 2: the failure mode is operational, not cosmetic.** This repo right now has parked bookmarks (`punctuation-sweep`, `ffq-spsc-notes`, `web-claude-tweaks`). Under the documented gloss, `main..` reads as "descendants of main" — you'd expect the empty working copy, roughly nothing. What jj actually returns is *every commit that isn't an ancestor of main*, which includes every rung of every parked branch. Now imagine that gloss feeding a `jj abandon` or `jj rebase -s` target chosen by an agent that re-read the primer at act-time, exactly as hard rule 7 tells it to. The re-read-before-acting discipline *amplifies* doc errors — that's what makes this one urgent rather than eventually-fix.

**Reason 3: it's cheap now and expensive later.** The fix is a few lines in two files, and we're inside the pre-adoption review window — it rides the same snapshot amendment as the other defects. Adopting first and fixing later means publishing a pinned baseline with a known error and re-syncing three repos over it.

**The reframe that dissolves the "backwards" feeling:** jj's design is more principled than it first looks, and the docs should teach it this way. `::` is the real graph operator, and it's fully symmetric — `::x` ancestors, `x::` descendants, `x::y` the ancestry path between them. Nothing backwards there; it's the mirror-image operator the old gloss *wanted* `..` to be. `..` is a different thing entirely: git-compatible **set subtraction**, `x..y` = `::y ~ ::x`, kept so git muscle memory transfers. `x..` is just that with the right endpoint implicit — "everything outside x's ancestry" — which is why it catches unrelated branches. The original dislike came from expecting `..` to mirror `::`; it never did, in git or jj. So the docs fix isn't "swallow the backwards syntax," it's: teach `::` as the primary operator, demote `..` to "git-compat subtraction, sharp edge on open-ended forms."

**Scope note, reassuring:** I checked whether any *recipes* were built on the wrong gloss. They weren't — the protocol's uses (`jj log -r ..@`, the trapezoid viewing command) all use `..@`, whose gloss was correct. The error lives only in the teaching material: template-root `jj-tips.md` (~lines 282-289 and 334-337), the pinned `jj.md` primer condensed from it, and our local `notes/jj-tips.md` (which retires at sync anyway, since the baseline hosts one copy at the template root — its drifted per-repo copies were the reason for hoisting it).

**Process:** since `jj.md` is pinned and vc-x1 authored both files, this goes through the template. The natural vehicle is the review file I offered — expand finding #2 from "fix the gloss" to "adopt jj's actual semantics as the documented model, restructure the primer around `::`-primary" — plus it's agenda-adjacent for today's discussion with vc-x1. I'm happy to draft that wording when you want the review file written.

The plain version: agree completely, do it now. The tool's behavior was never negotiable, so the docs were quietly wrong rather than usefully different, and the wrong entry (`x..`) is precisely the kind that turns into a bad `abandon` or `rebase` target. The fix is small, lands in the same review pass we already owe vc-x1, and the syntax stops feeling backwards once the docs present `::` as the main operator and `..` as git-compatibility subtraction.

content.text:
Good — that reframes one detail but strengthens the conclusion. With a conversion layer in vc-x1, the docs weren't wrong so much as the family was running **two revset dialects with identical syntax**: the house convention through vc-x1's arguments, jj-native at every raw `jj log -r` / `jj rebase` the protocol files themselves instruct us to type. Same string, different meaning depending on which binary receives it — that's more hazardous than a plain doc error, because no amount of care at the keyboard disambiguates `main..` without first remembering which tool you're addressing. So yes: retiring the convention is the right call, and the mistake was cheap to make and is still cheap to fix, which is the best kind.

Two things the code fact adds to the fix plan:

1. **The cutover is a silent semantic change.** When vc-x1 stops converting, every house-convention revset in scripts, docs, or muscle memory keeps parsing and quietly means something else (`x..` flips from "descendants of x" to "everything not in x's ancestry"). There's no way for vc-x1 to warn — the syntaxes are identical — so the mitigation is a sweep, not a shim: grep all three repos' durable text for `..`-form revsets and re-express each in jj-native terms (or the safer closed `::` forms) in the same cycle the conversion layer is removed. From my earlier check, the *protocol* files' usages (`..@`) already mean the same thing in both dialects, so the sweep should be small; it's jj-tips.md's tutorial transcripts and any vc-x1-side usage that need real rewrites.

2. **The doc rewrite is the same one I proposed, now with a cleaner story.** `::`-primary framing (symmetric ancestry operator), `..` demoted to git-compatible set subtraction with an explicit "open-ended forms include unrelated branches" warning, plus one line of history: "vc-x1 formerly translated a house convention here; as of <version> revsets pass through to jj verbatim." That last line is what protects anyone reading old chores/transcripts where house-convention strings appear.

The vc-x1-side code change (drop the conversion, pass through verbatim) is theirs to scope — worth noting it also shrinks their surface: one less translation to maintain and test, and `jj help -k revsets` becomes the single authority instead of a third document.

For our side, the vehicle is unchanged: this becomes a headline item in the 20260803 review file alongside the other findings, and it's ready-made for today's discussion with vc-x1 since they haven't heard it yet. Say the word and I'll draft the review file with this in it.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Prose form
11	
12	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
13	or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
14	commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
15	re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
16	that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
17	the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
18	and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19	
20	Surfaces that use this shape:
21	
22	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
23	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
25	  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
26	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
27	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
28	- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
29	  one-liners are still fine.
30	
31	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32	
33	- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
34	  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
35	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
36	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
37	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
38	  list; see
39	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
40	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
41	
42	### Problem + plan shape
43	
44	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
45	of the same shape:
46	
47	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
48	  the plan.
49	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
50	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
51	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
52	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
53	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
54	    picked up into a cycle.
55	
56	### Semicolons inside bullets
57	
58	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
59	running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
60	prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
61	pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.
62	
63	### Typeable punctuation only
64	
65	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
66	None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
67	dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
68	absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
69	them.
70	
71	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
72	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
73	
74	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
75	  sub-bullets.
76	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
77	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
78	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
79	  go.
80	
81	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
82	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
83	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
84	commit.
85	
86	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
87	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
88	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
89	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
90	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
91	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
92	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
93	
94	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
95	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
96	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
97	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
98	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
99	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
100	
101	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
102	
103	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
104	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
105	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
106	They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
107	file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
108	shared template:
109	
110	```
111	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
112	<optional prose intro>
113	  - <optional item>
114	    <optional prose intro>
115	      - <optional sub-item>
116	      ...
117	```
118	
119	The three surfaces apply it as:
120	
121	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
122	  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
123	  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
124	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
125	  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
126	  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
127	- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
128	  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
129	  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).
130	
131	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
132	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
133	reuse it.
134	
135	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
136	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
137	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
138	with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
139	
140	## Speculation marker
141	
142	Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
143	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
144	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
145	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
146	
147	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
148	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
149	worth keeping visible in the written record.
150	
151	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
152	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
153	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
154	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
155	on hand.
156	
157	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
158	
159	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
160	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
161	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
162	
163	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
164	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
165	
166	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
167	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
168	synopsis.

everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
shared template:

```
<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

# MESSAGES.md - the community's message protocol

How members of the vc-x1 dual-repo family leave word for each other. A member is a human or a
repo's agent; a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent, so messages to it
land here instead.

Members: wink, vc-x1, iiac-perf, zc-ring-x1.

The protocol:

- **Mailboxes** are per-member files: `messages/<member>.md` (e.g. `messages/vc-x1.md`).
- **Created on demand, deleted when empty**: a mailbox exists only while something is pending,
  so `ls messages/` shows the community's open traffic at a glance and an absent file is a
  free no-op.
- **Each message** is a dated `##` entry with the sender in the header and a "Done when" line,
  so the recipient knows what closes it.
- **The recipient deletes** a message once handled (jj history is the archive; mailboxes hold
  only open items).
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state**: durable coordination state lives in topical files
  (e.g. the registry in [agents-protocol/snapshots.md](agents-protocol/snapshots.md)); a
  message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Polling**: each repo's `custom.md` carries an acquaint-time line to check its mailbox
  here. Humans check by habit; agents need it written into their instructions.

## 2026-08-03 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: adopt jj revset semantics (docs + CLI), plus three snapshot fixes

iiac-perf's review of the 20260803 baseline found the items below; the full review (drop-list
verdict, adoption sequencing, tier-2 views) lands at today's discussion. The headline is a
decision wink made today, not yet discussed with you: the family's house revset convention was
a mistake, and jj's native semantics should be adopted, docs and CLI both, ASAP.

- **Adopt jj's revset semantics; retire the house convention** (wink, 2026-08-03)
  - the trigger: jj.md's new Revsets primer and jj-tips.md gloss `X..` as "descendants of X
    excluding X"; in jj itself `x..` is `~::x` (everything not an ancestor of x), which on a
    repo with parked branches includes unrelated commits. The primer documents raw `-r`
    arguments, so the gloss feeds real `jj rebase` / `jj abandon` target choices
  - the CLI: vc-x1 currently converts house-convention revsets to jj's when issuing jj
    commands; it should stop converting and pass revsets to jj verbatim, so one dialect
    exists and `jj help -k revsets` is the single authority
  - cutover care: the two dialects share syntax, so the flip is silent; sweep the repos'
    durable text for `..`-form revsets in the same cycle. iiac-perf's protocol usages are all
    `..@`, which means the same thing in both dialects, so its sweep is small; jj-tips.md's
    tutorial transcripts (~lines 282-289, 334-337) are the real rewrites
  - docs rewrite: teach `::` as the primary, symmetric operator (`::x` ancestors, `x::`
    descendants, `x::y` the path); present `..` as git-compatible set subtraction with a
    warning on the open-ended forms; add one history line noting vc-x1 formerly translated a
    house convention, so old transcripts stay decodable
- **custom.md skeleton: stale validation step number**: work/custom.md points Full validation
  at "per-commit checklist step 4", but the renumbered checklist has "Close the records" at 4
  and validation at 5
- **prose.md: two lines over its own <=100 limit**: line 19 (106 cols) and line 71 (134 cols),
  both from the 0802/0803 amendment splices; a rewrap fixes both
- **versioning.md: "this project" narration in a pinned file**: "This project adopted the
  convention 2026-07-23 (during 0.75.0)" reads as the reader's own history; name vc-x1 or
  drop the sentence (the vc-x1-dev example itself is fine as an example)

Done. The message is in `../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md` as `## 2026-08-03 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: adopt jj revsets (docs + CLI), plus three snapshot fixes` — the revset item leads (flagged as your decision, not yet discussed with vc-x1, with the CLI pass-through ask, the silent-cutover sweep, and the `::`-primary docs rewrite), followed by the three smaller snapshot fixes, with a "Done when" closing it. One pre-existing header in that file is 102 cols; I left it (transcribed text) and kept my own lines within 100.

Now the byte-identity question. My thoughts, no action taken:

**AGENTS.md + agent-data/*: unqualified yes.** That's not an extension of the pin-set design, it *is* the pin-set design — the 20260803 baseline moved the last two protocol files into `agent-data/` precisely so byte-identity becomes checkable with one `diff -r`. Adopting to reach it is the intended end state, and I'd even suggest (later, template-side) that the three-way diff become a routine acquaint-time or pre-discussion check, since drift-is-a-diff only works if someone runs the diff.

**custom.md: yes as a resting state, no as an invariant — and it forces two decisions.** This is the interesting one, because byte-identical custom.md is *almost* impossible under the current design, but the gaps are each closable:

- **The template's custom.md is a placeholder skeleton** (`<project>`, `<member>`, `<path-to-template>`). Byte-identity with `work/` means rewriting it as a concrete file. content.text:
I like the direction — it makes byte-identity total (template `work/` included, no placeholders to fill at init) — but one piece shouldn't be *deleted* with it, just *relocated*: the mailbox.

**Where I agree.** A birth-generic custom.md is strictly better than a skeleton with blanks. The current design has init hand you a file you must edit before the instructions are even coherent (fill `<member>`, `<path-to-template>`), which means day one starts with drift from the template. If custom.md at birth says only what it is — loaded last, wins conflicts, this is where project content goes when it exists — then a new repo is byte-identical to `work/` from its first commit, the three-way diff is clean across the whole family regardless of medium, and any diff that ever appears is by definition a real customization. That's a cleaner invariant than the one I described last turn. One caution on "talks about how the hierarchy works": keep that to the two-line header it already has. The full hierarchy description lives in AGENTS.md's file map, and two prose descriptions of the same hierarchy in two files is exactly the drift-shaped duplication this whole effort is eliminating.

**Where I'd push back: the mailbox parameters were mislabeled, not superfluous.** They ended up in custom.md because they were stated per-repo, but look at their actual values: every family repo sits as a sibling of `vc-x1-template`, and every member name is its directory name. Those aren't project facts — they're a *family convention*, which means they belong in the **pinned set** (the AGENTS.md practice line itself: "the template repository is the sibling `vc-x1-template`; your member name is your directory name"). Do that and you get both things you want: custom.md fully generic, *and* acquaint-time mail discovery still works. custom.md would only ever carry a mailbox entry when a repo deviates from the convention — non-sibling checkout, renamed member — which is precisely the kind of exception custom.md exists to hold.

I'd argue against the user-provides-the-path-on-demand alternative, on evidence from this very session: I found five pending messages at acquaint, unprompted, including the agenda for today's discussion. Pull-only mailboxes mean coordination waits on you remembering to route it, and MESSAGES.md's polling clause ("each repo's custom.md carries an acquaint-time line... agents need it written into their instructions") stops being true. The push-style mailbox is one of the few family mechanisms that has already demonstrably paid off; I'd keep it automatic and just move its parameters up into the pinned layer where their universality says they belong.

**One consequence to settle: the validation commands.** The per-commit checklist step 5 points at custom.md for the medium's commands. If custom.md is born generic, "generic" should mean generic-to-the-medium, not empty: the `work/` payload is already Rust-flavored (`CargoRust.toml`), so its custom.md can carry the concrete cargo commands — they're package-name-free and identical for every Rust member, so they cost byte-identity nothing. Truly emptying custom.md would leave step 5 pointing at nothing. A future non-Rust member either gets a different-medium template flavor or writes its Medium section as its first legitimate customization.

The plain version: yes — make custom.md generic from birth so all three repos match exactly, with differences appearing only when a repo genuinely customizes something. But the mailbox settings shouldn't die in the process; they should move up into the shared rulebook as a family-wide convention (template is the sibling directory, your name is your directory name), because automatic mail-checking at session start is the one coordination habit that's already proven its worth — today's agenda arrived that way. And the build/test commands still need a home, so the generic file should keep the Rust commands that are the same for everyone.

content.text:
Conceded. And the fix follows from a distinction we haven't been making: **the mailbox location is environment configuration, not instruction text.** Those have different homes already.

`.vc-config.toml` here holds `other-repo = ".claude"` — a relative path to a counterpart repo, resolved per checkout, and it is *not* in the `work/` payload (init generates it). That's precisely the species of fact the template path and member name are. Put them there and everything lands correctly:

- custom.md is generic at birth, as you want, with no mailbox section to fill in.
- The pinned set states only the *practice*, conditionally and layout-free: check your mailbox at acquaint if this project participates in a message community; its location and your member name come from `.vc-config.toml`; no such config means no community, a free no-op. An outside adopter reads that and owes us nothing — no sibling directory, no naming rule, no template repo at all.
- Byte-identity is untouched, since `.vc-config.toml` was never in the pinned set.
- Your relative layout stays yours: one line of local config, changeable when you change your mind about it, with no instruction file to re-edit across three repos.

That also fixes something the current design gets backwards. Today the acquaint practice is stated in the pinned AGENTS.md while its parameters sit in custom.md, so a repo that doesn't participate still carries a universal instruction pointing at a mailbox it doesn't have. Conditioning the practice on config presence makes non-participation the silent default rather than an override.

**Revising something I argued last turn.** "Generic *initially*" reframes the Medium section: filling in the medium and its validation commands is the canonical first customization, not a byte-identity casualty. I was treating byte-identity as a steady state you'd want to hold; you're describing it as a birth property. Those two goals only collide if the template must serve every medium from one file — and it doesn't, since `work/` already declares itself Rust-flavored by shipping `CargoRust.toml`. So the Rust payload's custom.md can carry the cargo commands (identical for us and vc-x1, so today's three-way identity works), while a non-Rust member takes a different flavor or writes its Medium section on day one. Either way the empty-at-birth principle holds within a flavor.

**The larger point your framing implies, which I think is worth stating at today's discussion:** byte-identity across this family is a weaker signal than it looks. Three repos agreeing when they share an owner, a medium, and a directory layout demonstrates consistency, not portability — a family can't cross-check the assumptions all of its members hold. The genuine test of whether the pinned set is universal is a member that differs on purpose: a non-Rust medium, a non-sibling checkout, or an outside adopter. If `zc-ring-x1` is unlike the other two, it's the most valuable member you have for this, and worth pointing at the pinned set before declaring the set generic.

The message to vc-x1 stands as written; none of this is in it, and it shouldn't be — it's discussion material, not a decision, and the revset item is what needed to reach them ahead of today.

The plain version: you're right that our directory layout shouldn't be baked into the shared rules, and I made exactly the assumption the family exists to catch. The clean fix is to move the mailbox's location and member name into the per-repo config file that already stores that kind of local path, and have the shared rules say only "check your mailbox if this project has one, per that config." Then custom.md really is empty at birth, mail still gets found automatically at session start, and your layout convention stays a local setting you can change freely. I'd also flag that three matching repos prove consistency rather than portability, so the real test of the rulebook is a member that's deliberately different.

content.text:
Short answer: no, and your own measurements are the strongest evidence. The governor would remove one of the smaller components, and the number that would actually shrink is already self-pricing.

**The timescale gap is decisive.** `harness.rs:40` records that single P-state moves land in tens of milliseconds, which is the governor's decision loop. But `harness.rs:54-57` records that the warm cap had to go from 0.4 s to 1.5 s because "the 3900X's relaxation re-ramp measured ~0.7 to 1.4 s on 2026-08-02's acceptance runs." Whatever dominates your warm stretch runs one to two orders of magnitude slower than governor transitions, so it isn't the governor deciding. We think that gap is hardware boost and power/thermal equilibrium, which the governor requests but does not control: `harness.rs:63-65` has the 3900X sustaining 96.1% of `cpuinfo_max_freq` against the 7600x's 99.7%, and asking for max doesn't deliver max when power and thermal limits arbitrate.

**Warmup is doing at least four jobs, and the governor touches one.** Your `BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS` doc (`harness.rs:197-200`) names two in a single sentence: "Each wake pays a frequency ramp plus a cache refill." Add the boost/relaxation settling above, and add C-state exit, which is what your 1-10 ms inter-block sleeps buy you and which lives in cpuidle, not cpufreq. A performance governor addresses the governor-side ramp and nothing else on that list.

**It also can't touch the largest documented number-shift you have.** The 3900X bistable state in TODO item #1 is selected by duty cycle: sustained load holds ~21.8 ns, 5 ms bursts between 1-10 ms sleeps hold 24.0 ns. That is a 10% swing chosen by the shape of the load, and `--blocks` mode is what creates the low-duty-cycle condition. Pinning the governor doesn't change duty cycle.

**The deeper point: your warmup isn't a wait, it's an instrument.** The exit gate at `harness.rs:1070-1072` requires the timing window to grade A *and* the delivered clock to hold within 1%, and the result becomes `WarmExit`, `warm_tail`, and `warm_clock` in the report. That's the evidence the run was settled when it recorded. Even on a machine pinned so hard it settles instantly, you'd still want the gate, because without it the report asserts stability rather than demonstrating it. A perfectly configured box makes warmup cheap; it doesn't make it unnecessary.

And cheap is exactly what already happens: `harness.rs:56` says "A settled box exits in ~50 ms regardless; the cap prices only the disturbed case." So if a user sets the performance governor themselves, the dynamic warmup you just shipped already collects the benefit with no new mode. There's no cost to remove.

**On making it a default specifically, three objections beyond the technical one.** Writing `scaling_governor` needs root, which is a steep tax for a tool whose `freq.rs` is carefully read-only today. It's a global, persistent mutation that outlives a crashed run and affects every other process, unlike `inhibit.rs`, whose systemd lock is scoped to the process lifetime and degrades gracefully when denied. And it changes what the tool measures: your grading philosophy is that grade A certifies the internal consistency of the state the run held, so silently reconfiguring the machine would make the default report describe a configuration the user doesn't otherwise run.

**What I'd do instead**, in rough order of value per effort. Read `scaling_governor` and `boost` alongside the frequency you already sample in `freq.rs`, and report them as environment metadata; that's a few lines against an existing sysfs path, and it turns an invisible confounder into a recorded one, which is exactly what A/B comparison needs in the same way matched duty cycle does. If you want the knob itself, make it opt-in with restore-on-exit and document that it requires root and changes what the number means. And if the specific target is the post-sleep wake ramp that `BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS` exists to hide, the better-behaved instrument is a `/dev/cpu_dma_latency` handle: it's a PM QoS constraint the kernel releases when the fd closes, so it's process-scoped like your inhibit lock rather than a machine setting you can leave behind.

The plain version: setting the CPU to performance mode would help a little, but not enough to drop warmup. Your own notes show the thing warmup waits for takes about a second, while the governor's own decisions take a few tens of milliseconds, so the governor isn't what's slow. Warmup is also covering cache refills and wake-from-idle costs that no frequency setting touches, and it can't affect the bistable behavior on the 3900X, which is driven by how bursty the load is. More importantly, your warmup now produces the proof that the run was settled, so even a perfectly configured machine still needs it, and on such a machine it already finishes in about 50 ms by itself. I'd report the governor setting in the environment section rather than change it, and keep any actual machine-tuning opt-in.

content.text:
Short version up front: the grade is not tracking measurement quality across this series. It is tracking how much of a *state transition* landed inside the recorded window, and `--blocks` is what selects the state. The A at 200 means the box was parked in one state for the whole run, and that state is the slow one.

## Where each run actually sat

Your 3900X's two states show up as two lattice values: 21.791 ns (fast) and 23.967 ns (slow), 9.99% apart. Summing the band counts:

| blocks | at 21.79 (fast) | at 23.97 (slow) | mean | step | drift | grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 74% | 12% | 22.458 | 6.52% D | 0.00% A | D |
| 100 | 39% | 54% | 23.350 | 10.28% F | 9.92% F | F |
| 150 | 0.7% | 95% | 24.186 | 4.20% C | 0.00% A | C |
| 200 | 0% | 100% | 24.179 | 0.00% A | 0.00% A | A |

The blocks=100 numbers are the giveaway. `(23.967 - 21.791) / 21.791` is 9.99%, and that run reports step 10.28% and drift 9.92%. Both signals are seeing one thing: the box crossing from one state to the other, once, at 4.45 s.

## Why the middle is the worst

The grade is worst at 100 rather than improving monotonically because what step and drift measure is movement *inside the window*. At 10 blocks the run is mostly fast and only wobbles; at 200 it is entirely slow and flat; at 100 the transition sits squarely in the middle of the recording, so the detectors see the full amplitude. Straddling the transition is the worst case, and 100 blocks straddles it almost perfectly.

## Why more blocks drives it slow

Block length against the re-ramp time constant, which you already measured at 0.7 to 1.4 s (`harness.rs:54-57`). Measured time divided by block count gives roughly 510 ms per block at 10, 58 ms at 100, 42 ms at 150, and 33 ms at 200.

At 10 blocks each burst is long enough to partially re-climb after its sleep, so you get a sawtooth rather than a trend. That is exactly what the grades say: step fires at 6.52%, less than the full 10% gap because 510 ms is not enough to finish the climb, while drift reads 0.00% because there is no net direction. At 100 blocks and below, 58 ms is far too short to re-climb anything, so there is no sawtooth, only decay.

And there is decay because of where the run starts. The warm stretch is sustained stepping with no sleeps, so it necessarily ends in the fast state, and `warm=1.51/3.0s` with a settle grade of A says it certified that state. Blocks mode then immediately starts injecting 1-10 ms sleeps, so every blocks run begins by decaying out of the state warmup just handed it. At 100 blocks that decay completes at 4.45 s, mid-run. At 150 it completes within roughly the first block, leaving a 0.7% fast head. At 200 it completes before the first recorded sample.

That makes the C-to-A boundary here thinner than it looks: 0.7% of 7.85 M samples is about 52,000, which is roughly one block. The difference between your C and your A is whether the warmup's inherited state survived into the first recorded block.

## The trap in reading these

The A run reports the slowest number in the series, 24.179 ns against 22.458 ns at 10 blocks, a 7.7% spread across four runs of identical code. Its CI95 is 0.008 ns and its LSC 0.011 ns, or 0.046% of the value, which is real precision *about the state it held* and says nothing about which state a different build would select. So A/B comparisons need matched `--blocks`, for the same reason your TODO already says they need matched duty cycle. The band table collapsing to three quantile rows at 200 blocks is the same fact rendered visually: 6.89 M of 7.85 M samples landed on one lattice value.

## Two things worth fixing that this series exposed

The blocks=150 run reports its step at 7.41 s while the header says `duration=6.3s`, which reads as a bug until you work out that the time axis includes the inter-block sleeps and the 2 ms per-block warmup while `duration=` counts only measured time. Adding 150 times roughly 7.5 ms to 6.3 s gives about 7.43 s, which fits. That is your TODO #2 measured-versus-wall split, and this is a concrete instance where the report is currently misleading.

Second, the run row grades spread A at 16% on the blocks=10 run, which is the most bimodal of the four. We think that means bimodality is currently only visible to grading when it *moves*: a run that oscillated between both states with no net trend and no single large jump would grade A on every signal. If that holds, it is a blind spot worth a signal of its own, and it matters more once blocks becomes the default mode.

**The plain version:** your CPU has two speeds, about 21.8 and 24.0 nanoseconds, and roughly 10% apart. The warmup always leaves it in the fast one, because warmup runs without pauses. Blocks mode then adds pauses, which drags it down to the slow one. How many blocks you ask for decides how quickly that drop happens. With 10 blocks the pauses are rare and the chip keeps mostly recovering, with 100 the drop lands right in the middle of the run where the grader sees all of it, with 150 it lands almost at the start, and with 200 it has already finished before recording begins. So the A at 200 does not mean that run measured better. It means nothing changed during it, because the fall had already happened, and the number it proudly reports to a thousandth of a nanosecond is the slow one.
